scenes: Since 2013, one logging feature let strangers run code, and nobody noticed.
Log4j is how Java programs keep a diary. Whatever your users type? Logged.
By default, Log4j quietly swaps special codes in a logged line for real values.
One code is risky. It makes Java fetch from any address the attacker names.
An attacker sends that text. Your server logs it, then fetches and runs their code.
Web requests get logged. The string hides in addresses or browser labels. Easy to hide.
Then in late 2021, Chen Zhaojun at Alibaba Cloud privately reported what nobody had spotted.
Apache rated the danger ten out of ten, the highest possible. Top of the scale.
Update your Log4j. The first fix limited lookups, and later versions switched JNDI off.
No patch? Filter outbound traffic. Your server can't fetch attacker code.
Verdict: nobody hacked Java. One logging feature obeyed strangers, exactly as designed.
Patch it, then ask what else your logs quietly obey, because
Claude Code sometimes put your email in web requests. Did that cause scam emails?
One user reports dozens of scam emails daily and blames Claude Code. That's his claim.
Claude kept inventing names for author tags. So the team gave it your email.
Claude's own curl web request sometimes carried your email. Not every time.
Some sites ask scripts for a contact. Yours was the only address Claude had.
Newer builds check web calls for your email. It's on by default.
Its README says page fetching, web search and plugin tools aren't checked.
Scripts Claude writes and runs itself slip past the check. That's the big gap.
The real fix removes your email from Claude's context in the next release.
Stable's still on an old build, so update to 2.1.317 or later. Check yours first.
Then open slash plugins and confirm that privacy add-on is switched on.
Don't wait for the next release, because the check misses scripts. Update your build.
Nobody's proven the spam link, but remember that
Pick NoSQL for speed? Then one username change becomes many rewrites.
People pick NoSQL for simple design and spreading across machines. Fair enough.
Most NoSQL databases cannot join tables, which is how SQL stitches related data together.
So you store copies. Each blog comment carries its author's username inside.
That saves you a lookup every time someone reads the comment. Reads stay quick.
Now your user renames their account. Many places need fixing. Ouch.
The rule: copies work best when reading happens far more often than writing.
Your product catalogue fits NoSQL. Constantly edited data does not. Simple as that.
Many NoSQL systems favor speed over matching copies. So you can read outdated data.
Another fix nests comments inside the post. One request returns them all. Neat.
Copies make renames costly. Choose NoSQL for speed only when your data rarely changes.
Speed always has a price, so before you choose, ask yourself whether to
AccuWeather halved its server load in 2011 by making its data worse.
Picture your phone asking for the forecast. Smartphone weather apps were swamping AccuWeather's servers.
You and a neighbor in the same area each triggered a separate request.
Then AccuWeather's servers chopped your GPS location down to fewer decimal places.
Nearby phones now looked identical, so one saved answer served them all.
That saved copy is a cache, and reading it beats asking the slower original.
The price was precision, because your exact spot stopped mattering to the server.
Daily trips to the server dropped by half. Half the work, gone.
The catch is stale data: when the original changes, your copy goes out of date.
Caches work because recent requests tend to repeat, and nearby ones tend to follow.
AccuWeather's result backs my verdict: for nearby users, worse data beats perfect data.
So before you buy more servers, never forget that
Your sale goes live and one machine decides everything.
Traffic floods in. A load balancer shares it, so no server drowns while others idle.
Round robin gives your servers turns. Each new request goes to the next in line.
Busy servers get a break. Least connections picks the server with the fewest active connections.
Another trick picks two servers at random and chooses the better one.
The hub decides. Fixed rules centre on a router, the master, handing out work.
Your master acts as a bottleneck, a narrow spot that slows everything down.
It cannot scale. As your traffic grows, very large servers quickly outgrow this design.
Dynamic designs check each server's current load. No node is set aside for distribution.
DNS helps too. The internet's address book can share traffic with no dedicated node.
Remember this: when your master chokes, your whole sale hangs on one machine.

Deleting your leaked key fixes nothing. GitHub's own docs say rotate it.
You delete the key and feel safe. But git remembers. It searches removed text.
A scanner called Gitleaks reads old commits too, hunting passwords, keys and tokens.
Your first move is simple. Rotate the key. Swap in a fresh one.
Once you rotate it, the old key opens nothing, whoever copied it.
Erasing history is different. It takes teamwork. Everyone who cloned your repo must coordinate.
Worse, rewriting history carries a high risk of the leaked data creeping back.
Check your exposure. Search history for the key. Git lists commits that touched it.
Before every commit, your scanner checks the change and blocks any secret it finds.
Here's the catch. You can skip that check by adding a prefix to the command.
So rotate first, then decide whether rewriting history is worth the trouble.
Rotate first, every single time, and never forget that
Did Stripe charge you twice when your payment timed out?
That fear is real. The payment can work, but your reply gets lost.
Your app invents a unique label, called an idempotency key, for each payment.
Retry with the same label and the server hands back its saved answer.
Stripe saves the first answer, even when that answer is a server error.
But some failures never get saved. Bad input and clashing requests run fresh.
Change a detail and the server says no. Same key, different payment, error.
Old keys expire, though. Past twenty four hours, they can be deleted.
The web is writing this down. Draft revision eight of the header is out.
Keys go on POST requests, which create things. Reading and deleting repeat safely already.
Replay the first answer and a retry never charges you twice.
